title: Proof, Viewpoint, and Debate
objectives: I can use argument, viewpoint, and proof to explain what makes a case strong.
I can judge whether a speaker or source is logical, convincing, and trustworthy.
I can use on the other hand and in conclusion to organize what I say and write.
I can debate a question by giving reasons for more than one side.
rationale: Fifth graders begin argument writing, and they need names for its parts before they can use them. The unit pairs the structure words (argument, viewpoint, proof, debate) with judgment words (logical, convincing, trustworthy, one-sided) and two transition phrases that organize a speech or essay. It follows the connotation unit so that students already know that word choice shows feeling. Every later unit's argue task reuses these words.

words.def: A set of reasons given to show that an idea is right or wrong.

senses.example: The two friends had an argument about whose turn it was.

words.ex: Her argument for a longer recess listed three reasons and a fact from a study.
words.ex2: In a good argument, every reason supports the claim.
words.nonExample: Shouting "Because I said so!" is not a strong argument.

morph.note: The final e of argue is dropped before -ment.

words.rel: the case you build with reasons

apps.academic: A written argument has a claim, reasons, and evidence.
apps.spoken: That is a good argument, but I have another point.
apps.writing: In school writing, an argument is a claim supported with reasons, not a quarrel.

cloze.s: The class's ___ for a longer lunch period included a survey of eighty students and a map of the crowded cafeteria.

cloze2.s: Her ___ was strong because each reason was backed by a fact from a reliable book.

misuse.s: A good argument in writing is a fight where students yell at each other.
misuse.why: In school writing, an argument is reasons that support a claim, not a yelling match.

visual.alt: A set of scales beside a speech bubble.

words.def: To discuss a question by giving reasons for different sides.
words.ex: The two classes will debate whether schools should start later in the morning.
words.ex2: My cousins debate every Sunday whether soccer or basketball is the better sport.
words.nonExample: Two people who only shout at each other are not really debating.

apps.academic: In social studies, students debate how a historical choice could have turned out differently.
apps.spoken: Let's debate it: I say pizza, and you say tacos.
apps.writing: Use debate as a verb for a respectful contest of reasons.

cloze.s: The council members will ___ the new park plan for an hour, with one group giving reasons to build it and another giving reasons to wait.

cloze2.s: In class, we ___ whether homework helps, and each team must give two reasons.

misuse.s: We will debate by agreeing with every person and never giving any reasons.
misuse.why: To debate is to discuss different sides with reasons; agreeing with everyone and giving none is not debating.

visual.alt: Two students speaking across a table with scales between them.

words.frame: We can debate whether ___ by giving reasons such as ___.

words.def: A person's way of thinking about a topic; an opinion.
words.ex: From the farmer's viewpoint, the rain was a gift; from the camper's, it ruined the weekend.
words.ex2: A good reporter shares more than one viewpoint on a story.
words.nonExample: A fact, like the date of a holiday, is not a viewpoint.

segs.m: a way of seeing or thinking

morph.note: A compound word made of two words.

words.rel: where you stand on a topic

apps.academic: A historian compares the viewpoint of a settler with the viewpoint of a native nation.
apps.spoken: From my viewpoint, the first plan is better.
apps.writing: Use viewpoint to name how a character or an author sees an issue.

cloze.s: From my little brother's ___, bedtime at eight is unfair, but my parents think it is fair.

cloze2.s: The author told the story from the dog's ___, so a giant vacuum cleaner seemed like a terrifying monster.

misuse.s: A viewpoint is a measurement, like how many inches tall a desk is.
misuse.why: A viewpoint is a way of thinking about something, not a measurement.

visual.alt: An eye looking at a mountain from one side.

words.def: Facts or evidence that show something is true.
words.ex: The footprints in the mud were proof that someone had walked through the garden.
words.ex2: Before I believe it, I need proof, not just a rumor.
words.nonExample: A rumor you heard in the hallway is not proof.
words.rel: facts that back up a claim

apps.academic: In math, a proof shows step by step why a statement must be true.
apps.spoken: Do you have proof, or is that just a guess?
apps.writing: Use proof for solid facts that settle a claim.

cloze.s: The receipt was ___ that Maria had paid for the book on Tuesday.

cloze2.s: Without ___, the detective could not tell the mayor who had taken the painting.

misuse.s: Proof is a guess with no facts behind it.
misuse.why: Proof is made of facts that show something is true; a guess has no facts.

visual.alt: A checked document that confirms something.

words.def: Making sense because each step follows from the one before.
words.ex: It is logical to bring an umbrella when the forecast says storms are coming.
words.ex2: Her logical plan put the heaviest boxes on the bottom shelf and the lightest on top.
words.nonExample: Wearing shorts because it is snowing is not a logical choice.

apps.academic: A logical argument moves from facts to a conclusion without gaps.
apps.spoken: That makes logical sense to me.
apps.writing: Use logical to praise ideas in which each step follows the last.

cloze.s: Because the road was flooded, the ___ choice was to turn around and take a different route.

cloze2.s: Sam gave a ___ explanation: the plant was wilting because no one had watered it for two weeks.

misuse.s: It is logical to wear a winter coat to the beach on a sunny day in July.
misuse.why: Logical means it makes sense; a heavy coat on a hot beach does not.

visual.alt: Puzzle pieces joined by an arrow.

words.def: Strong enough to make people believe it.
words.ex: The lawyer gave a convincing speech that made the jury nod.
words.ex2: A convincing poster shows real facts and a clear picture.
words.nonExample: A story full of mistakes is not very convincing.

apps.academic: A convincing paragraph gives a reason and then proof for it.
apps.spoken: That was convincing; I changed my mind.
apps.writing: Use convincing for evidence or a speaker that earns belief.

cloze.s: The student's ___ speech included two facts, a short story, and a clear request, and the whole class voted yes.

cloze2.s: The magician's trick was so ___ that even the teacher believed the coin had vanished.

misuse.s: Her convincing argument was so weak that nobody believed a single word.
misuse.why: Convincing means strong enough to make people believe; an argument nobody believes is not convincing.

visual.alt: A speaker at a microphone while the audience gives a thumbs up.

words.def: Safe to believe or depend on; honest and reliable.
words.ex: The trustworthy guide always told hikers the truth about the weather.
words.ex2: A trustworthy website names its author and shows where its facts come from.
words.nonExample: A page with no author and no sources is not very trustworthy.

segs.m: belief that someone is honest or reliable

morph.note: Trustworthy ends in -y; worthy is worth + -y.

apps.academic: To check whether a source is trustworthy, ask who wrote it and how they know.
apps.writing: Use trustworthy for people and sources that deserve belief.

cloze.s: The librarian showed us how to find ___ sources: books by experts and websites that list where their facts came from.

cloze2.s: Because Omar always returned what he borrowed and kept every promise, everyone thought he was ___.

misuse.s: A trustworthy friend often lies and breaks promises.
misuse.why: Trustworthy means you can depend on someone; lying and breaking promises is the opposite.

visual.alt: A handshake beside a locked padlock.

words.frame: I think a source is trustworthy when ___.

words.def: Showing only one point of view and ignoring the rest.
words.ex: The article was one-sided because it never mentioned the other team's reasons.
words.ex2: Mia wanted a fair report, not a one-sided story that only praised her school.
words.nonExample: A report that explains both teams' reasons is not one-sided.

apps.academic: A one-sided source leaves out evidence that does not match its claim.
apps.spoken: That review feels one-sided; it never says anything bad.
apps.writing: Use one-sided to point out what an author left out.

cloze.s: The news story felt ___ because every quote came from the company and none came from the neighbors.

cloze2.s: A ___ review gives only the good things about a game and hides every problem.

misuse.s: The report was one-sided because it explained both teams' reasons equally.
misuse.why: One-sided means showing only one side; explaining both teams equally is balanced.

visual.alt: A scale tipped far down on one side.

words.def: A phrase that introduces a different or opposite point.
words.ex: I love apples; on the other hand, I do not like apple juice.
words.ex2: The trip sounds exciting. On the other hand, it costs more than we saved.
words.nonExample: It does not fit between two ideas that agree.

apps.academic: Writers use on the other hand to show the opposite side of a topic.
apps.spoken: I like that plan; on the other hand, it is expensive.
apps.writing: Put a comma after on the other hand when it begins a sentence.

cloze.s: Soccer is fun to play with a team; ___, biking lets me ride alone at my own speed.

cloze2.s: Mr. Ortiz said the old bike was cheap; ___, the new one would last for years.

misuse.s: I love chocolate cake; on the other hand, chocolate cake is my favorite dessert.
misuse.why: On the other hand introduces a different or opposite idea; here the second idea agrees with the first.

visual.alt: Two open hands, each holding a different idea.

words.frame: I like ___; on the other hand, ___.

words.def: A phrase that begins the final summary of what was said.
words.ex: In conclusion, recess helps students focus, share, and stay healthy.
words.ex2: She wrote, in conclusion, that the old library deserves to stay open.
words.nonExample: Starting a speech with this phrase would confuse the listeners.

apps.academic: An essay's last paragraph often begins with in conclusion and restates the claim.
apps.spoken: In conclusion, I think we should go.
apps.writing: Use in conclusion only at the end, then restate your claim in fresh words.

cloze.s: Her essay listed three reasons, and the last paragraph began with ___ to signal the final summary.

cloze2.s: The talk had gone on for an hour, so the audience cheered when the speaker said ___ and began her final summary.

misuse.s: He began his whole speech with in conclusion and then introduced three brand-new topics.
misuse.why: In conclusion belongs at the end of a talk, not the beginning.

passage.title: The Empty Lot
paras: Ms. Alvarez's class was ready to debate a question: should the school plant a garden on the empty lot? Each team had to build an argument, and each argument needed proof.

Team One spoke first. Their viewpoint was that a garden would feed families and teach science. They showed a photo of the lot, a list of vegetables, and a letter from a farmer, a trustworthy expert. Their plan was logical: students would plant in spring, water twice a week, and harvest in fall.

Team Two disagreed. "A garden costs money, and who will water it in summer?" asked Dani. "On the other hand, a soccer field would cost less, and every student could use it." The class thought Team One had been convincing, but Ms. Alvarez noticed a problem. "Your talk was one-sided," she told Dani gently. "You gave no proof that a field would cost less."

Dani nodded and brought a price list the next day. By Friday, both teams had changed their plans: a garden on half the lot and a small field on the rest. Maya, from Team One, gave the final speech. "In conclusion," she said, "two viewpoints made our plan stronger than either one alone."

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the phrase "one-sided" describes a talk that
choices: shows only one point of view
qs.why: Ms. Alvarez says Dani gave no proof for the other side of her plan, so one-sided means showing only one point of view.

qs.q: Why did Dani bring a price list the next day?
choices: She wanted to leave class early.
She wanted proof for her claim that the field would cost less.
She wanted to join Team One.
She was angry at Ms. Alvarez.
qs.why: Ms. Alvarez said Dani lacked proof, so the price list is the proof she was missing.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that Team One used a trustworthy source?
choices: They showed a photo of the lot.
They included a letter from a farmer, an expert.
They planned to harvest in fall.
qs.why: A letter from an expert is a source people can depend on.

qs.q: What is the central idea of the passage?
choices: Gardens are cheaper than soccer fields.
Teams should never change their plans.
Listening to different viewpoints can lead to a better plan.
qs.why: Both teams changed their plans, and Maya says two viewpoints made the plan stronger.

write.frame: My viewpoint is that ___. One piece of proof is ___. In conclusion, ___.

adds a different viewpoint with a reason
constructed.model: The brochure was one-sided: it only listed the fun parts of the camp. On the other hand, former campers said the cabins were cold and the food was bland.

teacher.overview: Students learn the language of fair argument: the parts (argument, viewpoint, proof, debate), the ways to judge them (logical, convincing, trustworthy, one-sided), and two phrases that organize a speech or essay. They apply the words in a class-debate narrative and in short oral and written arguments.

notes.va.argument.n: Distinguish the school sense (a claim with reasons) from the everyday sense (a quarrel). The senses entry shows both. Model with a claim and two reasons on the board.
notes.va.debate.v: A verb: discuss a question by giving reasons for sides. Model respectful turns with sentence frames. A debate does not need a winner.
notes.va.viewpoint.n: A compound: view + point. Use a picture seen from two sides (a house from the front and the back) to show that different positions give different views.
notes.va.proof.n: Proof means facts that settle a claim; students often use it for any support. Ask: could this convince a stranger, or only a friend?
notes.va.logical.adj: Each step follows from the one before. Give a chain such as 'storm, so flooded road, so detour' and then one with a missing step.
notes.va.convincing.adj: Convincing relates to the effect on listeners. A speaker can be convincing and still wrong; follow with a check for proof.
notes.va.trustworthy.adj: A compound: trust + worthy. Practice sorting sources by author, date, and listed sources.
notes.va.one-sided.adj: Not the same as 'wrong': a one-sided source may be accurate but incomplete. Ask what was left out.
notes.va.on-the-other-hand.phr: A transition phrase that signals contrast. Rehearse with 'I like ___; on the other hand, ___.' and with a comma after it at the start of a sentence.
notes.va.in-conclusion.phr: Signals the final summary. Show a paragraph that opens with it and a paragraph that uses it in the wrong place.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'My claim is that recess should be longer. My argument has two reasons: students focus better, and they get exercise. For proof I will use a study from a trustworthy source. On the other hand, some people worry about lost class time, so I need an answer. In conclusion, I will repeat my claim in new words.'
discuss: What makes you trust one source more than another?
Can a strong argument change your mind even when you wanted to disagree?
misconceptions: An argument is always an angry fight.
Proof and opinion mean the same thing.
A convincing speaker must be right.
A one-sided source is always lying.
extend: Compare two short articles on one topic and decide which is more trustworthy and why.
Hold a short class debate with a rule: each speaker must restate the other side before giving a reason.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit with a quick-write two days later: claim, one reason, one proof. Return to the unit's words each time students argue in later units, and connect assertive and inquisitive from unit 1.

frames: My argument is that ___ because ___. As proof, ___.
From my viewpoint, ___. On the other hand, ___.
I think this source is trustworthy because ___. I think it is one-sided because ___.
wida.oral: Partner A states an opinion and one reason. Partner B says "On the other hand," and gives the opposite side with a reason. Then both say "In conclusion" and sum up what they learned.
